title: Error Handling
subtitle: Handling HTTP errors, network failures, timeout, and parsing error responses
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: fetch() only throws for network failures, not HTTP errors. Without proper error handling, 4xx and 5xx responses silently pass through, and UI shows stale or no data without telling the user what went wrong.
whyItExists.solution: Check response.ok after every fetch. Parse the error body (APIs return structured error objects). Distinguish network errors (no internet) from HTTP errors (server responded with an error). Implement retry logic for transient failures.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every fetch() call — no exceptions. All API calls can fail.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't retry all errors — only 429, 502, 503, 504 are worth retrying. Never retry 4xx errors (400, 401, 403, 404, 422) — retrying won't fix a client-side mistake.

explainModes.beginner: There are two kinds of API failures: network errors (no internet — fetch throws an Error) and HTTP errors (server replied with an error status — fetch does NOT throw, you check response.ok). Always use try/catch around fetch calls. Inside, check if (!res.ok). Parse the error body to show the user a useful message.
explainModes.simple: try { const res = await fetch(url); if (!res.ok) { const err = await res.json().catch(() => ({})); throw new Error(err.message || res.statusText); } return await res.json(); } catch (err) { if (err.name === 'TypeError') { // network error } else { // HTTP error } }. 401 = not logged in. 403 = logged in but no permission. 404 = resource not found. 422 = validation failed. 429 = rate limited. 5xx = server error (retry later).
explainModes.standard: Error response parsing: most APIs return JSON: { error: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'User 42 not found' }. Some return HTML on 500. Use .catch() on res.json() to handle non-JSON error bodies. Retry with exponential backoff: retry 5xx errors after 1s, 2s, 4s... up to 3 attempts. Always add jitter (random delay) to avoid thundering herd. AbortController for timeout: wrap fetch with a timeout signal — catch AbortError specifically. Custom error classes: class ApiError extends Error { constructor(status, body) { ... } } — lets you instanceof check.
explainModes.technical: Retry decision: network errors (TypeError) = retry. 500, 502, 503, 504 = retry (transient server issues). 429 = retry after Retry-After header delay. 4xx (except 429) = don't retry (client mistake). Structured error response format: RFC 7807 'Problem Details' — { type: URI, title, status, detail, instance }. Used by many REST APIs. AbortSignal.timeout(): new in modern browsers — AbortSignal.timeout(5000) creates a signal that aborts after 5 seconds. Cleaner than manual AbortController + setTimeout.
explainModes.deepDive: Circuit breaker pattern: after N consecutive failures, stop sending requests for a cooldown period (circuit 'opens'). After cooldown, try one request (half-open). If it succeeds, close the circuit. Prevents hammering a failing service. Dead letter queue: failed requests that exhausted retries go to a queue for manual review or later replay. Correlation IDs: include a unique X-Request-ID header — if an error occurs, include the ID in your error report so the API provider can find it in their logs. OpenTelemetry: structured tracing across multiple API calls — see exactly where latency or errors originate.

questions.question: You receive a 429 Too Many Requests response. What should you do?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds
Check the Retry-After response header for how long to wait, then retry after that delay with exponential backoff
Treat it as a permanent error and stop all API calls forever
Switch to a different endpoint to avoid the rate limit
questions.explanation: 429 means you've exceeded the API's rate limit. The Retry-After header (if present) tells you exactly how many seconds to wait before retrying. Without that header, use exponential backoff: wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s. Never retry in a tight loop — you'll hit the rate limit again immediately and potentially get your IP banned. Most APIs have separate rate limits per endpoint, user, and IP — switching endpoints doesn't help.

faq.q: How do I show the user a helpful error message instead of 'HTTP 422'?
faq.a: Parse the error body from the API response — most APIs return a structured JSON error: `{ "error": "VALIDATION_FAILED", "message": "Email is invalid" }`. After checking `!res.ok`, do `const errBody = await res.json().catch(() => null)`. Then use `errBody?.message || res.statusText` as the user-facing message. For 422 Validation errors, many APIs also return a list of field-specific errors — render those next to the relevant form fields.

examples: Stripe returns structured errors: { error: { type, code, message, param } } — parse param to highlight the right field
GitHub returns X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset — implement retry-after logic
OpenAI returns { error: { message, type, code } } — display message.message to users
